title: Month-over-month change

WITH m AS (
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(ShipDate), MONTH(ShipDate), 1) AS MonthStart,
           SUM(ShipmentValue) AS Total
    FROM oil.Shipments
    GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(ShipDate), MONTH(ShipDate), 1)

SELECT MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart)         AS PrevMonth,
       Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart) AS Change
FROM m

title: Top 3 sites per region by shipment value

WITH t AS (
    SELECT p.Region, p.SiteName, SUM(e.ShipmentValue) AS TotalShipmentValue,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.Region ORDER BY SUM(e.ShipmentValue) DESC) AS rn

    JOIN oil.Sites AS p ON p.SiteID = e.SiteID
    GROUP BY p.Region, p.SiteID, p.SiteName
)
SELECT Region, SiteName, TotalShipmentValue
FROM t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY Region, rn;

title: Monthly rank of carriers
q: For each month, rank carriers by their total shipment value that month and show only the top carrier (ties included).
sql:
WITH m AS (
    SELECT MONTH(e.ShipDate) AS MonthNo, d.CarrierName, SUM(e.ShipmentValue) AS Total,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY MONTH(e.ShipDate) ORDER BY SUM(e.ShipmentValue) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM oil.Shipments AS e
    JOIN oil.Carriers AS d ON d.CarrierID = e.CarrierID
    GROUP BY MONTH(e.ShipDate), d.CarrierID, d.CarrierName
)
SELECT MonthNo, CarrierName, Total
FROM m
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY MonthNo;

title: Repeat shipments within N days
q: Find shipments that happened within @Days days of the same site's previous shipment. Use @Days = 145. Show site, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT SiteID, ShipmentID, ShipDate,
           LAG(ShipDate) OVER (PARTITION BY SiteID ORDER BY ShipDate, ShipmentID) AS PrevDate
    FROM oil.Shipments
)
SELECT SiteID, PrevDate, ShipDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, ShipDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, ShipDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY SiteID, ShipDate;

title: Constraint vs trigger vs app
q: Write a query that shows, for each table, how many PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints it has.
sql:
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS TableName,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'PK' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS PK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'F'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'UQ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UQ,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'C'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'D'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DF
FROM sys.objects
WHERE type IN ('PK', 'F', 'UQ', 'C', 'D')
  AND SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) = 'oil'
GROUP BY parent_object_id
ORDER BY TableName;
how: Prefer declarative constraints: they are faster, always applied, and help the optimizer. Use triggers only for cross-table rules, and application checks for friendly messages.

title: Shipment chain for one site
q: Starting from site 1's first shipment, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that site's shipments in date order, with a step number.

WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT ShipmentID, ShipDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ShipDate, ShipmentID) AS rn
    FROM oil.Shipments
    WHERE SiteID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT ShipmentID, ShipDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.ShipmentID, o.ShipDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1
    FROM Ordered AS o
    JOIN Chain AS c ON o.rn = c.rn + 1
)
SELECT ShipmentID, ShipDate, Step
FROM Chain
ORDER BY Step;

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 200
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS HowMany, MAX(n) AS LastNumber
FROM N
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);

title: Top 3 products by spend per region

title: Month-over-month with a calendar
q: For all 12 months of 2024 (even empty ones), show total shipment value, previous month's total and growth %.
sql:
WITH Months AS (
    SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS date) AS m
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(month, 1, m) FROM Months WHERE m < '2024-12-01'
), Totals AS (
    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.ShipmentValue), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN oil.Shipments AS e
           ON e.ShipDate >= mo.m AND e.ShipDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)
    GROUP BY mo.m
)
SELECT m AS MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))
            / NULLIF(LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0) AS decimal(6,1)) AS GrowthPct
FROM Totals
ORDER BY m;

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > site) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.
sql:
DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM oil.Sites
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.SiteID, r.NodeID, p.SiteName
FROM oil.Sites AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.SiteID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

title: MERGE: sync a staging table
q: Sync product prices from a staging list: update prices that changed, insert new products, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (ProductID int, ProductName nvarchar(80), ProductCode varchar(20), PricePerUnit decimal(12,2));
INSERT INTO @Stage VALUES
    (1,  N'Acetaminophen 325mg tablet', 'LUBE-00001', 0.09),   -- price change
    (2,  N'Acetaminophen 500mg tablet', 'LUBE-00002', 0.10),   -- no change
    (51, N'Loratadine 10mg tablet',     'LUBE-00051', 0.12);   -- new

MERGE oil.Products AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.ProductID = s.ProductID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.PricePerUnit <> s.PricePerUnit THEN
    UPDATE SET t.PricePerUnit = s.PricePerUnit
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (ProductID, ProductName, ProductCode, PricePerUnit)
    VALUES (s.ProductID, s.ProductName, s.ProductCode, s.PricePerUnit)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.ProductID, deleted.PricePerUnit AS OldCost, inserted.PricePerUnit AS NewCost;
how: MERGE does insert, update and (optionally) delete in one statement. The extra `AND t.PricePerUnit <> s.PricePerUnit` skips rows that did not change. $action in OUTPUT reports what happened to each row. MERGE must end with a semicolon.

title: Generate test rows with a set

     UnitCount, ShipDate, DispatchedAt, RecordedAt, CarrierID)

       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01' AS date)),
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01 09:00' AS datetime2(3))),
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01 09:01 +00:00' AS datetimeoffset(3))), 1
FROM N;

FROM oil.Shipments
WHERE ShipmentID BETWEEN 1001 AND 1020;

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = @@SPID;
how: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED (the default) prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantom rows. title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each site's total shipment shipment value and total number of shipment items. Make sure the shipment value is not double counted.
sql:
SELECT p.SiteID, p.SiteName,
       ISNULL(ch.TotalShipmentValue, 0) AS TotalShipmentValue,
       ISNULL(li.ShipmentItems, 0) AS ShipmentItems
FROM oil.Sites AS p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT SiteID, SUM(ShipmentValue) AS TotalShipmentValue
           FROM oil.Shipments
           GROUP BY SiteID) AS ch ON ch.SiteID = p.SiteID
LEFT JOIN (SELECT e.SiteID, COUNT(*) AS ShipmentItems
           FROM oil.ShipmentItems AS r
           JOIN oil.Shipments AS e ON e.ShipmentID = r.ShipmentID
           GROUP BY e.SiteID) AS li ON li.SiteID = p.SiteID
ORDER BY TotalShipmentValue DESC;
how: If you join Shipments and ShipmentItems first and then SUM(ShipmentValue), a shipment with 2 shipment items has its shipment value counted twice (fan-out). Aggregating each child table separately before joining fixes this. Interviewers often test whether you spot fan-out.

title: Short-circuit is not guaranteed
q: Return products where the name has a space and the text before the first space is longer than 8 characters. Write it safely so CHARINDEX never gives a negative length.
sql:
SELECT ProductName
FROM oil.Products
WHERE CASE WHEN CHARINDEX(' ', ProductName) > 0
           THEN LEN(LEFT(ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', ProductName) - 1))
           ELSE 0
      END > 8;
how: SQL Server does not promise to evaluate AND conditions left to right, so `CHARINDEX(...) > 0 AND LEN(LEFT(... - 1)) > 8` could still error on a row with no space. A CASE expression controls the order. This is a senior-level detail.

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find shipments that are not a parent of any other shipment, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oil.Shipments AS e
   WHERE e.ShipmentID NOT IN (SELECT ParentShipmentID
                               FROM oil.Shipments)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oil.Shipments AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM oil.Shipments AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentShipmentID = e.ShipmentID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentShipmentID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. NOT EXISTS ignores the NULLs and correctly finds that no shipment is a parent. You can also fix NOT IN by adding `WHERE ParentShipmentID IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

title: Rank without window functions
q: Rank products by unit cost (1 = most expensive) using a correlated subquery instead of RANK().
sql:
SELECT m.ProductName, m.PricePerUnit,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oil.Products AS x
        WHERE x.PricePerUnit > m.PricePerUnit) + 1 AS CostRank
FROM oil.Products AS m
ORDER BY CostRank, m.ProductName;
how: A row's rank is 1 + the number of rows with a higher cost. That gives the same result as RANK(), ties included.

title: Top site per region
q: Using only subqueries (no window functions), show the site with the highest total shipment value in each region.
sql:
SELECT t.Region, t.SiteName, t.Total
FROM (SELECT p.Region, p.SiteName, SUM(e.ShipmentValue) AS Total
      FROM oil.Sites AS p
      JOIN oil.Shipments AS e ON e.SiteID = p.SiteID
      GROUP BY p.Region, p.SiteID, p.SiteName) AS t
WHERE t.Total = (SELECT MAX(t2.Total)
                 FROM (SELECT p2.Region, SUM(e2.ShipmentValue) AS Total
                       FROM oil.Sites AS p2
                       JOIN oil.Shipments AS e2 ON e2.SiteID = p2.SiteID
                       GROUP BY p2.Region, p2.SiteID) AS t2
                 WHERE t2.Region = t.Region)
ORDER BY t.Region;
how: Per-site totals are compared with the maximum total of the same region. It works, but the window-function version is shorter, which is a good point to make in an interview.

title: Shipments after a site's first shipment item
q: For each site who has a shipment item, count how many of their shipments happened after the shipment of their first shipment item.
sql:
SELECT x.SiteID, COUNT(e.ShipmentID) AS LaterShipments
FROM (SELECT e1.SiteID, MIN(e1.ShipDate) AS FirstRxDate
      FROM oil.ShipmentItems AS li
      JOIN oil.Shipments AS e1 ON e1.ShipmentID = li.ShipmentID
      GROUP BY e1.SiteID) AS x
LEFT JOIN oil.Shipments AS e
       ON e.SiteID = x.SiteID
      AND e.ShipDate > x.FirstRxDate
GROUP BY x.SiteID
ORDER BY LaterShipments DESC, x.SiteID;
how: The derived table finds each site's first shipment item date. The LEFT JOIN on a date condition counts the later shipments, and sites with none get 0.

title: IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN
q: Return sites with at least one Pending shipment three ways (IN, EXISTS, JOIN with DISTINCT). Each should return the same count.
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oil.Sites
   WHERE SiteID IN (SELECT SiteID FROM oil.Shipments
                       WHERE Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaIn,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oil.Sites AS p
   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM oil.Shipments AS e
                 WHERE e.SiteID = p.SiteID AND e.Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaExists,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.SiteID)
   FROM oil.Sites AS p
   JOIN oil.Shipments AS e ON e.SiteID = p.SiteID
   WHERE e.Status = 'Pending') AS ViaJoin;
how: All three give the same answer. A plain JOIN repeats a site for each matching shipment, which is why DISTINCT is needed. IN and EXISTS never duplicate rows.

title: Products priced above their group's average
q: Products come in families (the first word of the name, e.g. 'Ibuprofen'). List products that cost more than the average of their own family.
sql:
SELECT m.ProductName, m.PricePerUnit
FROM oil.Products AS m
WHERE m.PricePerUnit > (SELECT AVG(x.PricePerUnit)
                    FROM oil.Products AS x
                    WHERE LEFT(x.ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', x.ProductName) - 1)
                        = LEFT(m.ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', m.ProductName) - 1))
ORDER BY m.ProductName;
how: The family is computed with LEFT + CHARINDEX (text before the first space). The correlated subquery averages only products of the same family.
